articles.title: Lame-duck Congress faces a short, crowded calendar as Democrats prepare to take over
articles.excerpt: Republicans have only a few weeks left with full control of Washington. Government funding, a defense policy bill and a doubtful push for a party-line spending package are all fighting for floor time.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
articles.imageCaption: The U.S. Capitol in Washington, where lawmakers return for a post-election session
articles.imageAlt: The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C.
content: With Democrats set to take over both chambers of Congress in January, Republicans have one stretch left to use the majorities they still hold: the post-election session known as the lame duck. The to-do list is long, the calendar is short, and the party is not entirely agreed on how hard to push.

The biggest decision sits with Senate Majority Leader John Thune. As [The Hill reported](https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/6185385-democrats-win-senate-midterms/), the South Dakota Republican has to choose between two uses of limited time. He can spend most of the session confirming as many of President Trump's nominees as possible, or he can devote weeks to a budget reconciliation package that would fund the Defense Department over Democratic objections. Reconciliation matters because it lets a party move spending and tax measures with a simple majority, no Democratic votes required.

Neither path looks easy. Thune has said it would be difficult to find the votes for another reconciliation bill with Republicans holding such slim margins, according to analysis from the [Center for Strategic and International Studies](https://csis.org/analysis/fy-2027-defense-funding-potential-post-midterm-outcomes). Calendar math makes it harder still. A bill can only be assembled after a budget resolution is adopted, and the number of days both chambers will actually be in session is small. One Senate Republican aide told [The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/house/6185340-gop-lame-duck-congress-2026-midterms-trump-agenda/) that reconciliation is "more unlikely than not."

The money at stake is not small. The president has asked for $350 billion in mandatory defense funding as part of a proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget for fiscal 2027, and the [Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget](https://crfb.org/blogs/lame-duck-session-shouldnt-be-excuse-borrow-more) estimates that Congress could consider as much as $420 billion in additional defense spending during the lame duck, perhaps as part of a reconciliation package.

Then there is the work Congress cannot skip. The current stopgap spending measure runs out in December, so lawmakers have to pass full-year appropriations or kick the can with another short-term bill. The same Hill reporting lists a farm bill, a food aid package and the annual National Defense Authorization Act among the other items waiting in line. A group of Republicans wants to stretch the session as long as possible to pass as much of the party's agenda as they can while they still hold the gavels.

Nominations are the other pressure point. Senate Democrats have warned that Trump's judicial and executive branch picks will have a hard time getting confirmed, and starting in January they will have the votes to stop them. NBC News noted that the new majority could also matter for the Supreme Court, since several Democratic senators said before the election that they would be reluctant to confirm any Trump nominee to a vacancy in his final two years.

Leadership changes are coming on both sides of the Capitol. Thune is expected to be elected Senate minority leader when Republicans hold their leadership vote next week, and Chuck Schumer is expected to win the majority leader post when Senate Democrats meet in early December. Some incoming senators, including Illinois' Juliana Stratton, have said they may not back him. In the House, Speaker Mike Johnson is on track to hand the gavel to Democrat Hakeem Jeffries.

Republicans did not go into Election Day short on resources. A Republican source told The Hill that Thune and allied outside groups spent close to $750 million trying to protect the Senate majority. That effort fell short, and now the question is how much of the party's remaining time and leverage gets spent before the new Congress is sworn in.

articles.title: Democrats win control of the House and Senate in a midterm rebuke of Trump
articles.excerpt: Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats and the House, taking states Trump carried by double digits in 2024, as voters weighed in on his second term.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
articles.imageCaption: Voters across the country cast ballots in Tuesday's midterm elections
articles.imageAlt: Voters casting ballots at a polling place on Election Day
keywords: Senate flips Texas Ohio Maine North Carolina
content: Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, giving the party a firm grip on Congress when the new session opens in January. The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats late Tuesday night and the House early Wednesday morning, according to [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/saradorn/2026/11/04/midterm-election-results-live-updates-democrats-sweep-house-and-senate-in-stunning-rout/). [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/03/politics/live-news/midterm-election-congress), CBS News and NBC News had projected the outcome earlier, and the coverage widely described it as a rebuke of President Donald Trump.

The House margin was still being worked out. Network projections of the final Democratic total ranged from roughly 230 to 255 seats, according to SBS News, and every estimate was well past the 218 needed. [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/democrats-capture-full-control-congress-nbc-news-projects-fueled-victo-rcna607042) said the party could end up with its largest House majority in nearly two decades. Hakeem Jeffries of New York is poised to become Speaker and would be the first Black person to hold the job, though the incoming House still has to elect him when the new Congress convenes.

The Senate was the bigger surprise. Republicans started the night with a 53-47 majority, and Democrats needed a net gain of four seats. That looked like a long shot for most of the cycle because the competitive races were mostly in states Trump won comfortably in 2024. By Wednesday morning Democrats had flipped seven Republican-held seats: Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa, North Carolina, South Carolina and Maine. Forbes reported that the AP made the Senate call after Democrat Josh Turek beat Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa.

Several of the wins came with real names attached. Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper beat Trump-endorsed Michael Whatley, flipping the seat of retiring Sen. Thom Tillis. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted. In Texas, state Rep. James Talarico beat Attorney General Ken Paxton, ending a Democratic losing streak of more than three decades there, and in Kansas the Rev. Adam Hamilton ousted Sen. Roger Marshall, becoming the first Democrat Kansas has sent to the Senate since 1932. In South Carolina, Annie Andrews defeated Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed after the death of her brother Lindsey Graham in July. In Maine, Troy Jackson defeated Sen. Susan Collins, ending her nearly 30 years in the chamber.

Democrats also held open seats in Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire, and Jon Ossoff won re-election in Georgia, according to AP calls reported by Forbes and [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/election-day-2026-midterms/).

Exit polls pointed to the reasons. A CNN exit poll found about 60% of voters disapprove of Trump's job performance, and roughly 90% said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote. An AP exit poll found about 60% believed the United States made the wrong decision in attacking Iran, and about a third called the war crucial to their congressional vote, Forbes reported. Democrats ran on affordability and what they called a culture of corruption, while Republicans leaned on the tax-cut law passed last year, [The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/6185385-democrats-win-senate-midterms/) reported. In several states Trump had personally picked the nominee, sometimes over objections from inside his own party.

Republicans did try to protect themselves. Trump and his allies pressed GOP-led states to redraw congressional maps, and Decision Desk HQ reported that the effort gained the party a few seats it otherwise would have lost. It was not enough against the national mood.

A Democratic majority changes what Congress can do right away. House Democrats will control committees and can issue subpoenas, and MS NOW reported that their oversight list includes immigration enforcement, federal spending decisions and the use of executive power. In the Senate, Democrats will be in a position to block Trump's nominees. Chuck Schumer is expected to be elected majority leader when Senate Democrats hold their leadership vote in early December.

The night was not a clean sweep in every contest. Republican Byron Donalds won the Florida governor's race, beating Democrat David Jolly, and Sen. Ashley Moody held her Florida seat. A few races, including some House contests, were still uncalled early Wednesday, so final seat totals could shift.

articles.title: Trump says he will accept the midterm results and work with Democrats, but keeps his veto threat
articles.excerpt: As Democrats took Congress, the president said he was open to deals, blamed his absence from the ballot for Republican losses and stopped short of fully backing Speaker Mike Johnson's future in leadership.
articles.author: fiveboroughbulletin-staff
articles.imageCaption: The White House, where President Trump watched election returns on Tuesday night
articles.imageAlt: The White House seen from the North Lawn in Washington, D.C.
content: President Donald Trump said Tuesday night that he is willing to accept the midterm election results and work with Democrats, even as he made clear he intends to use his veto pen. Speaking to The New York Times shortly before 10:30 p.m. Eastern while watching returns at the White House, he said he was "absolutely willing" to accept the outcome, according to [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/live-blog/midterm-election-results-2026-news-trump-live-updates-rcna605763).

The conciliatory tone came after a very different message earlier in the day. In an interview with [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/election-day-2026-midterms/) before polls closed, Trump said he held what he called the ultimate power, the veto, and he embraced the nickname "Mr. Veto" for a Congress under Democratic control. Later, on a Politico livestream, he said he would work with Democrats but would not hesitate to veto bills he did not like. Before the vote, he had said he would accept the results if the elections were honest.

Trump put the blame for Republican losses on his own absence from the ballot. In a social media post he wrote that he would have won in a landslide had he been on it. Time reported that he railed against the Democratic victories in a series of Truth Social posts Tuesday evening, so his tone was not uniformly conciliatory. A White House official told Fox News that candidate quality mattered and that the president had promoted many of the candidates better than they promoted themselves. Trump also told the Times that he did not regret endorsing Ken Paxton in Texas. Paxton lost his Senate race to Democrat James Talarico.

The president was asked about the future of House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is set to hand the gavel to Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries in January. Trump called Johnson's tenure a very good job but would not fully endorse him to remain the House Republican leader in the minority. Johnson, for his part, blamed the party's losses on historical precedent, which is that the president's party usually loses ground in midterm elections.

Jeffries, who is positioned to become the first Black Speaker, used his victory speech to frame the night as a demand for change. He said voters had made clear that they were tired of extremism and corruption and described House Democrats' priority as an affordable America, according to NBC.

The veto threat has limits. Overriding a presidential veto takes a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate, a bar Democrats are nowhere near clearing. That gives Trump real leverage in any negotiation, but it also means he will need Democratic votes to pass almost anything of his own in the next two years. His remark that the two sides would "probably work something out" will be tested quickly.

The first real test comes before the new Congress is even sworn in. Government funding expires in December, and Republican leaders are also weighing how much of the president's agenda they can push through the lame-duck session. Democrats, meanwhile, have already signaled that oversight of the administration, including its immigration enforcement operations and federal spending decisions, will be a central part of their work once they hold the majority.
